title: India's Textile Stocks Just Surged — and Brokerages Say the Sector's Best Years Are Ahead
excerpt: Motilal Oswal initiates coverage on eight textile companies with buy ratings and up to 39 percent upside, as cotton duty exemptions, China Plus One sourcing and new free trade deals create a once-in-a-decade opportunity for India's $194 billion textile industry.
body:
India's textile sector had a week that investors have been waiting years for. Shares of leading exporters — Gokaldas Exports, Pearl Global Industries, Welspun Living, Arvind and Indo Count Industries — surged between 3.7 and 11.2 percent after brokerage Motilal Oswal initiated coverage on eight textile and apparel companies with bullish buy ratings and price targets implying up to 39 percent upside.

The report, released this week, argues that India's textile industry is entering a structural inflection, not a cyclical bounce. Three forces are converging: the global "China Plus One" sourcing shift, India's improving trade architecture, and a massive capex cycle by domestic manufacturers.

## The China Plus One Dividend

India currently accounts for only 4 to 5 percent of global textile and apparel trade — a number that understates the country's manufacturing capacity by a wide margin. As global brands aggressively diversify supply chains away from China, India is emerging as a primary alternative alongside Vietnam and Bangladesh.

But recent tariff developments have levelled the playing field. India initially faced US tariffs as high as 50 percent in mid-2025, which were subsequently reduced to 10 percent until the end of July. Meanwhile, Bangladesh and Indonesia each secured arrangements at 19 percent, and Vietnam at 20 percent. The convergence has placed India on par with its key competitors in the US market.

"With India accounting for only 4-5 per cent of global apparel trade, significant opportunities remain to gain market share as global brands diversify sourcing beyond China," said Soham Samanta, research analyst at Motilal Oswal.

## The Stocks in Play

Motilal Oswal's coverage is concentrated on companies with scale, compliance readiness and export infrastructure — the attributes global buyers now prioritise:



> **"Three forces are converging: the global "China Plus One" sourcing shift, India's improving trade architecture, and a massive capex cycle by domestic manufacturers."**


**Gokaldas Exports** (Buy, target ₹1,110): Revenue CAGR of 18 percent, EBITDA CAGR of 33 percent and adjusted profit CAGR of 73 percent projected over FY26–28. Growth driven by India expansion and improved utilisation in Africa following the renewal of AGOA.

**Arvind** (Buy, target ₹670): Shifting from fabric to garments to expand its addressable market. Advanced materials division supports profitability. Revenue, EBITDA and profit CAGR of 15, 23 and 29 percent respectively.

**Pearl Global Industries** (Buy, target ₹2,300): Capacity expansion across India, Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia. Revenue, EBITDA and profit CAGR of 14, 25 and 29 percent.

**Indo Count Industries** (Buy, target ₹550): India's bed-linen export champion, benefiting from the emerging utility bedding segment. Revenue CAGR of 20 percent, with EBITDA CAGR of 44 percent — the strongest margin expansion story in the group.

**Welspun Living** (Buy, target ₹190): Integrated home textile manufacturer with longstanding relationships with global retailers. Positioned for gains from premiumisation and sustainability-led sourcing.

KPR Mill, Trident and Vardhman Textiles received neutral ratings — solid companies, but priced closer to fair value.

## The Cotton Tailwind

Adding to the momentum, the Indian government suspended the 11 percent customs duty on cotton imports from June 1 through October 31, 2026. The move immediately reduced raw material costs for spinning mills, garment exporters and home textile manufacturers. On the day of the announcement, textile stocks rallied 5 to 13 percent across the board.

For a sector where cotton accounts for 50 to 60 percent of input costs, the duty relief directly improves margins in the near term while better cotton availability supports production scaling.

## Trade Deals Are the Long Game

The structural case extends beyond this quarter. India's recently signed free trade agreement with the United Kingdom and an advancing EU trade deal are expected to reduce tariff barriers for Indian textile exports into two of the world's largest consumer markets.

The Indian government has set a target to scale the domestic textile market from $194 billion in FY26 to $350 billion by FY30 — a compound annual growth rate of 13 percent. Export expansion alone is targeted at 22 percent CAGR. Budget 2026's Mega Textile Parks initiative, cotton and man-made fibre support and the Tex-Eco sustainability programme are providing the policy scaffolding.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For diaspora investors watching from the US, the textile sector offers a rare combination of structural growth and attractive valuations. Most of the buy-rated stocks trade at single-digit or low-teens price-to-earnings multiples on FY28 estimates — a sharp contrast to Indian IT stocks at 20x-plus or consumer names at 40x-plus.

The risks are real: currency fluctuations, cotton price volatility, and execution risk on capacity expansion. But the sector's fragmentation — the top four or five players account for only 15 to 28 percent of export sales — means the consolidation runway is long.

As the brokerage noted, India's textile sector has historically punched below its weight. The combination of trade architecture, cost advantages and scale investments may finally be changing that equation.

*Sources: Motilal Oswal Research (June 2026), Hindu Business Line, LiveMint, CII-Kearney Report, Ministry of Finance notification (May 30, 2026).*
